domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents (OpenHands) in software-engineering workflows, covering agent loops, PR ownership, code review, and day-one use cases. OpenHands is a coding-assistant platform for software builders, fitting both coding_assistants and its parent developer_platforms. The content centers on practical adoption and effective use of coding agents in real development workflows rather than research or evaluation design. Requires basic familiarity with software development and LLMs but is accessible to practitioners without deep ML expertise. This is a single-speaker conference session from the AI Engineer channel. All evidence anchors are graded said_in_transcript, directly quoting the speaker.

summary: Robert Brennan introduces coding agents and their effective use, drawing on his experience building OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin). He frames a key thesis: while coding—typing code into an IDE—is going away, software engineering is not. Engineers will shift from writing code to thinking about user needs, business objectives, and architecture. AI excels at the write-run-iterate loop but struggles with big-picture tasks requiring empathy and organizational context. He defines a coding agent as software possessing agency—taking real-world actions through a code editor, terminal, and web browser—and contrasts agents with tactical tools like Copilot autocomplete. Under the hood, an agent is a loop between an LLM and the external world: the LLM proposes actions, the system executes them, and outputs feed back into the next turn. Each core tool has non-trivial design challenges: editors use find-and-replace or diff-based editing; terminals must handle long-running, parallel, and background commands; and browsers benefit from markdown conversion, accessibility trees, or labeled-node screenshots. Sandboxing via Docker and least-privilege credential scoping are essential safety measures. For best practices, Brennan advises starting small with single-commit tasks having clear definitions of done, being explicit about frameworks and methods, and treating code as disposable—prototyping freely and discarding failed attempts. Critically, he stresses that all AI-generated code must be reviewed: organizations that auto-merge without review accumulate tech debt, duplicate code, and breakage. He advocates a trust-but-verify mindset with humans always in the loop. He shares OpenHands' lesson that when PRs appeared as agent-owned, they languished and bypassed code review; now the triggering human's identity appears on the PR, ensuring accountability. Brennan catalogs high-value day-one use cases: resolving merge conflicts (99% success rate), addressing PR feedback, fixing quick bugs, infrastructure changes like Terraform, database migrations with proper best practices, fixing failing tests, expanding test coverage, and building internal greenfield apps where review rigor can be relaxed. He reports 90% of his own code flows through agents.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Thesis
sections.summary: Brennan introduces himself and OpenHands. He argues coding is going away but software engineering is not; engineers will spend more time thinking about user needs and architecture while AI handles the write-run-iterate loop.

sections.title: What Is a Coding Agent?
sections.summary: Defines agents by their agency—taking real-world actions through a code editor, terminal, and web browser. Contrasts agents with tactical codegen tools like Copilot autocomplete, noting agents are more asynchronous and powerful, working 5–15 minutes autonomously.

sections.title: How Agents Work Under the Hood
sections.summary: Explains the core agent loop: LLM proposes an action, system executes it in the real world, output feeds back into the LLM for the next turn. This understanding helps build intuition for effective agent use.

sections.title: Core Tools: Editor, Terminal, Browser
sections.summary: Details design challenges for each tool. Editors use find-and-replace or diff-based editing for efficiency. Terminals must handle long-running, parallel, and background commands. Browsers benefit from markdown conversion, accessibility trees, or labeled-node screenshots; a recent contribution doubled browsing accuracy.

sections.title: Sandboxing and Safety
sections.summary: Agents run in Docker containers by default to prevent dangerous actions. When granting API access (GitHub tokens, AWS), credentials must be tightly scoped following least-privilege principles.

sections.title: Best Practices: Start Small
sections.summary: Advises starting with small, quick tasks with a clear definition of done—fixing failing tests, lint errors, merge conflicts. As intuition grows, larger tasks become feasible. Brennan reports 90% of his code goes through agents.

sections.title: Best Practices: Be Explicit
sections.summary: Tell the agent not just what to do but how—specify frameworks, TDD strategies, exact file names. This improves accuracy, speed, and token efficiency by reducing unnecessary codebase exploration.

sections.title: Best Practices: Code Is Cheap
sections.summary: Encourages treating AI-generated code as disposable. Prototype freely, discard failures, and start fresh with improved prompts rather than over-iterating on fundamentally flawed agent output. Brennan voice-prompts ideas on his commute and merges or discards the resulting PRs 50/50.

sections.title: Review Code and Trust but Verify
sections.summary: Stresses that reviewing AI-generated code is the most important advice. Organizations that auto-merge without review accumulate tech debt and duplicate code. Advocates trust-but-verify: agents are consistent, but humans must remain in the loop, pulling and running code to confirm problems are actually solved.

sections.title: PR Ownership and Accountability
sections.summary: Shares OpenHands' lesson: when PRs showed as agent-owned, humans could self-approve and bypass code review, and PRs languished without ownership. Now the triggering human's face appears on agent-generated PRs, making them responsible for merging and any downstream breakage.

sections.title: Day-One Use Cases
sections.summary: Catalogs high-value agent use cases: resolving merge conflicts (99% success), addressing PR feedback, fixing quick bugs from Slack, infrastructure changes with Terraform, database migrations with proper best practices, fixing failing tests, expanding test coverage, and building internal greenfield apps where review rigor can be relaxed. Closes by inviting listeners to join the OpenHands community on GitHub, Slack, and Discord.

demonstrations: Brennan describes using OpenHands with voice prompts during his walk to work to generate PRs by the time he arrives.
Brennan shows an example of fixing a text-input-to-number-input bug directly from Slack without opening an IDE.
Brennan demonstrates addressing PR feedback by telling OpenHands to implement a frontend engineer's specific React-related requests.
Brennan describes resolving merge conflicts by simply asking OpenHands to fix conflicts on a PR, succeeding 99% of the time.

Agent-owned PRs languish without human ownership and can bypass code review systems
